claims.claim: In one inner-city geriatric clinic population, 9% had unrecognised BPPV, linked with lower ADL scores, a recent fall and depression.
claims.supporting_passage: We performed a cross-sectional study to determine the prevalence of unrecognized benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) and associated lifestyle sequelae in a public, inner-city geriatric population. ... Nine percent were found to have unrecognized BPPV. ... Patients with unrecognized BPPV were more likely to have reduced activities of daily living scores, to have sustained a fall in the previous 3 months, and to have depression.
claims.pico_timeframe: Older patients at one US public inner-city geriatric clinic / unrecognised BPPV / those without / ADL, fall in previous 3 months, depression / cross-sectional
claims.safe_wording: In one US study of patients at an inner-city clinic for older people, about 9 in 100 had BPPV that nobody had recognised. Those with it were more likely to have had a fall in the previous three months, though a single snapshot study cannot show that BPPV caused the falls.
claims.qualifications: One clinic, one country, year 2000; not a general prevalence; association only; sample size not given in abstract.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Prevalence varies across settings; no newer source checked in this batch.

numbers.meaning: proportion of the clinic sample with unrecognised BPPV (cross-sectional; denominator not in abstract)

claims.claim: Posterior canal BPPV is diagnosed with the Dix-Hallpike manoeuvre, and clinicians should treat it (or refer) with a canalith repositioning procedure; the guideline recommends against routine vestibular suppressant medicines.
claims.supporting_passage: The update group made strong recommendations that clinicians should (1) diagnose posterior semicircular canal BPPV when vertigo associated with torsional, upbeating nystagmus is provoked by the Dix-Hallpike maneuver ... and (2) treat, or refer to a clinician who can treat, patients with posterior canal BPPV with a canalith repositioning procedure. ... The update group made recommendations against ... (3) routinely treating BPPV with vestibular suppressant medications such as antihistamines and/or benzodiazepines. ... (3) assess patients with BPPV for factors that modify management, including impaired mobility or balance, central nervous system disorders, a lack of home support, and/or increased risk for falling
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 18+ with suspected BPPV, any setting / guideline recommendations
claims.safe_wording: The US ENT guideline (AAO-HNS 2017) strongly recommends diagnosing the commonest type of BPPV with the Dix-Hallpike test and treating it with a repositioning manoeuvre such as the Epley, and advises against routinely treating BPPV with sedating anti-dizziness medicines such as antihistamines or benzodiazepines. It also asks clinicians to assess falls risk and mobility.
claims.qualifications: US guideline; the named suppressants are antihistamines and benzodiazepines, not prochlorperazine specifically.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: The side-lying test adaptation for people with neck or back problems is NOT verified here (full text not opened); omit or source separately.

numbers.meaning: Dix-Hallpike head turn and neck extension

claims.claim: The Epley manoeuvre is effective for posterior canal BPPV.
claims.supporting_passage: Complete resolution of vertigo occurred significantly more often in the Epley treatment group when compared to a sham manoeuvre or control (odds ratio (OR) 4.42, 95% confidence interval (CI) 2.62 to 7.44; five studies, 273 participants); the proportion of patients resolving increased from 21% to 56%. ... There is a high recurrence rate of BPPV after treatment (36%). ... Some patients were unable to tolerate the manoeuvres because of cervical spine problems.
claims.pico_timeframe: Adults 18-90 with posterior canal BPPV / Epley / sham or control / complete resolution of vertigo / short follow-up
claims.safe_wording: In trials, about 56 in 100 people had complete resolution of vertigo after the Epley manoeuvre, compared with about 21 in 100 after a sham manoeuvre or no treatment. BPPV often comes back (about a third in these trials), and some people with neck problems could not tolerate the manoeuvre.
claims.qualifications: Mostly small trials, short follow-up; not specific to frail older people.

numbers.meaning: complete resolution, Epley vs sham/control, 5 trials, 273 participants

claims.claim: Prochlorperazine causes drowsiness and movement side effects in older people (BNF).
claims.safe_wording: Do not name prochlorperazine; say the guideline advises against routinely using sedating anti-dizziness medicines.

claims.claim: In a hospice EEG study, all 5 patients recorded when unresponsive showed a brain response (MMN or P3a) to tone changes, and 2 showed a P3b to pattern changes.
claims.supporting_passage: Consistent with control and responsive participants, all (5/5) showed some evidence of either an early fronto-central negativity (MMN), or a later fronto-central positivity (P3a), or both, to tone changes. None of the unresponsive patients showed a centro-parietal positivity (P3b) to the tone changes. One unresponsive patient (20%) showed evidence of a weak late fronto-central positivity (P3a) to pattern changes, and two patients showed stronger centro-parietal positivity (P3b) to pattern changes. ... The patient analysis to be described is based on nine patients (four female, age 28 to 88 years, mean age 68.2 years). Eight patients were recorded when they were responsive, five when they were unresponsive.
claims.location: Full text, Results and Methods (Hospice patients)
claims.pico_timeframe: Canadian hospice patients (mostly cancer, most on opioids, no delirium or cognitive impairment at entry) recorded when unresponsive (PPS 10%) / auditory oddball tones / compared with 17 young controls / event-related potentials / hours to days before death
claims.safe_wording: In a small Canadian study, researchers recorded brain activity in 5 hospice patients who had stopped responding and were close to death. All 5 showed brain responses to changes in simple tones, and 2 showed a response that in healthy people goes with consciously noticing the change.
claims.qualifications: Only 5 unresponsive patients (9 patients analysed overall, 13 recruited); no delirium at entry; mostly cancer; not a test of understanding speech.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Authors state it is unclear how these responses relate to conscious awareness; MMN is considered automatic.

numbers.meaning: unresponsive patients with MMN or P3a to tone changes
unresponsive patients with P3b to pattern changes
patients analysed (8 responsive sessions, 5 unresponsive); 13 recruited

claims.claim: These responses show the hearing system was working but do not show understanding.
claims.supporting_passage: Whereas the MMN (and perhaps too the P3a) is considered an automatic response to auditory irregularities, the P3b is associated with conscious detection of oddball targets. ... It is still unclear how the partial functioning of the auditory change detection system we have reported here relates to normal conscious awareness ... lends some credence to the advice that loved ones should keep talking to a dying relative as long as possible.
claims.safe_wording: The study shows the ear and brain were still reacting to sound; it does not show that the person understood words or knew who was there. The authors say it lends some support to the advice to keep talking to a dying relative.
claims.conflicting_or_uncertain: Small single study; not replicated in this batch.

claims.claim: Care guidance for the last days of life advises continuing to talk to the dying person.
claims.location: Not found (NICE NG31 and hospice leaflets not openable)
claims.safe_wording: Do not cite guidance; present speaking to the person as the authors' suggestion and as a judgement ('we should').

claims.claim: High-dose glucocorticoids should start immediately in active GCA.
claims.supporting_passage: We recommend that a suspected diagnosis of LVV should be confirmed by imaging or histology. High dose glucocorticoid therapy (40-60 mg/day prednisone-equivalent) should be initiated immediately for induction of remission in active giant cell arteritis (GCA) or Takayasu arteritis (TAK).
claims.safe_wording: European (EULAR) recommendations say high-dose steroid (prednisolone 40 to 60 mg a day) should start immediately in active giant cell arteritis, and that the diagnosis should be confirmed by imaging or biopsy.
claims.qualifications: Abstract does not explicitly say 'before confirmation' or 'on suspicion' or 'same-day fast-track'; BSR 2020 text (which says this) was not opened.

claims.claim: BSR 2020: ultrasound/biopsy time windows after steroids start; higher dose or IV methylprednisolone for visual symptoms; visual loss usually permanent; vague systemic presentations in older people.
claims.location: Not opened (no abstract, no PMC full text, not in Drive)
claims.safe_wording: Do not state time windows, visual-symptom dosing or permanence figures until the BSR guideline text is opened.

claims.claim: Dual sensory loss is common in older people and each loss reduces the usual workarounds for the other.
claims.supporting_passage: In combination dual sensory loss occurs. Dual sensory loss is becoming a more common condition seen by clinicians and previous research has shown that 6% of non-institutionalized older adults had a dual sensory impairment, whilst 70% of severely vision-impaired older adults also demonstrated a significant hearing loss. Decreased vision and/or hearing acuity interferes with reception of the spoken message and hence people with sensory loss frequently experience communication breakdown.
claims.safe_wording: Losing both sight and hearing is not rare in older people, and poorer sight or hearing both make it harder to follow speech. Avoid percentages (secondary figures from 2002).
claims.qualifications: Figures are cited from earlier research, not this review's findings.

claims.claim: English Care Act deafblind guidance requires councils to identify people and arrange a specialist assessment; Scotland's See Hear framework.
claims.location: Not opened (official web pages blocked; not in Drive)
claims.safe_wording: Omit until the guidance text is opened.

candidates.reason: Core claims supported (Oghalai with qualifications; AAO-HNS guideline; Cochrane). Prochlorperazine/BNF claim not checked, and the judge's side-lying test adaptation is not verified.
candidates.revised_angle: Keep: ask about positional triggers, Dix-Hallpike, Epley (56 vs 21 in 100 resolved; recurrence about a third). Say the guideline advises against routine sedating anti-dizziness medicines (antihistamines, benzodiazepines) without naming prochlorperazine. Present 9% as one US clinic sample, association with falls only. For frail people, only say the Cochrane review notes some people with neck problems could not tolerate the manoeuvre; do not describe the side-lying test unless sourced.

candidates.reason: Full text confirms numbers (5 unresponsive patients; 5/5 MMN or P3a to tone changes; 2 P3b to pattern changes) and the limits. 'Most' in the abstract understates the small numbers; use actual counts. Guidance claim dropped; practical advice framed as judgement and authors' suggestion.

Only immediate high-dose steroid (EULAR abstract) is supported. BSR time windows, visual-symptom dosing, permanence and older-person presentation were not verified because the BSR guideline could not be opened.
candidates.revised_angle: Either open the BSR 2020 guideline (Rheumatology 2020;59:e1-e23, doi 10.1093/rheumatology/kez672) in a later pass, or narrow the post to: in suspected active GCA, start high-dose steroid immediately (EULAR) and arrange urgent confirmation by imaging or biopsy. No time-window or dose-for-visual-symptoms figures.

candidates.reason: Reserve. The statutory deafblind-assessment claim (the angle's key ask) could not be opened; the dual-loss workaround point is only partly supported by an old narrative review.
candidates.revised_angle: Usable as fallback for C14-18 only if the DH 2014 deafblind policy guidance is opened; otherwise limit to the practical point: ask about sight when assessing hearing and vice versa, without statutory claims or percentages.
